newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp morning update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp morning update.

text.p: NEW DRAMA IN QUEENSLAND POLITICS
There's been another sensational development in Queensland politics this morning.

The Opposition has tabled a draft private members bill to try to force the hand of the Government to get Kenneth Carruthers to complete his inquiry into the deal between the State Coalition and the Police Union.
Mr Carruthers resigned on Tuesday, saying he couldn't continue because of interference from a Government-initiated judicial review of Queensland's Criminal Justice Commission.
Independent MP Liz Cunningham, who holds the balance of power in the house, says she had intended supporting the bill, but is now unsure about her position.
Premier Rob Borbidge says he's not sure how the government would vote if the bill was brought before the house.
The ALP's bill will be introduced into parliament in a fortnight.
MINISTERS MEET OVER HOUSING
Commonwealth and State Housing Ministers meet today to seek ways to reduce waiting lists for public housing.
The Melbourne meeting will try to make further progress on a new joint housing agreement, which has been worked on by a task force of officials.
While the Commonwealth believes agreement is close, some states have concerns about a Federal Government proposal for rent subsidies.
NEW CREDIT CODE TO PROTECT CUSTOMERS
Customers will be better protected when they choose a loan, as the Uniform Consumer Credit Code comes into force.
States and Territories have moved to ensure customers are better informed when taking out a personal loan.
The code was first proposed more than ten years ago.
Implementing the code has been a costly excercise for lenders, involving computer systems, new documents and staff training.
Former Banking Ombudsman, and now a manager at Westpac, Susan Brooks, says the banks alone have made a substantial investment to be ready for today, at a cost of over a hundred-million dollars.
WOODCHIP LICENCES ANNOUNCED
Greens Senator Bob Brown says the announcement of three-year woodchip export licences has set the seal of fastest destruction of Australian forests in history.
The government has announced 6.25 million tonnes of woodchips can be exported each year for the next three years, the largest volume ever.
More than half will come from Tasmania.
The Forest Industries Association says the woodchip export licences will create jobs and mean no more trees are cut down.
DOCTORS TO PROTEST TODAY
As of today, new doctors will have to be in an approved training programme to qualify for a medicare provider number, the key to general practice.
Junior doctors say that means hundreds of students have had their career paths removed, and they'll hold a national day of action.
Talks with Health Minister Dr Michael Wooldridge have failed to resolve the dispute.
Last month, the Minister said talk of action was just a threat.
The Australian Medical Association has promised only minor disruption to medical services, with elective surgery in some states cancelled.
PARCEL TRAVELLED TO NZ ON QANTAS FLIGHT
New Zealand police have confirmed that a parcel bomb that injured two students yesterday had travelled to New Zealand on a Qantas flight from Kuala Lumpur.
A Malaysian university student and her twenty-five year old friend suffered burns to their face, arms and legs after opening the parcel in a car outside a post office.
They were admitted to Lower Hutt Hospital's burns unit near Wellington and are expected to be discharged later tomorrow.
Interpol are hunting for a man in Malaysia whom police believe sent the bomb.
They say he is the only suspect being sought.
A Qantas spokeswoman refused to say today how the parcel slipped through the system saying it was the airline's policy not to comment on security.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 3873-1800
